764.title: Dry bread and cool water
764.hook: eat your dry bread, drink cool water, and don't envy another's buttered bread (Farid salok, ang 1379)
764.howItsDone: Farid's saloks are read and sung in gurdwaras with the rest of Gurbani; Sikhs read this couplet as a teaching against envy and greed, alongside the langar, the free kitchen where everyone eats the same simple food together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, collar: the clever mind told to bow and look within before marking anyone. Your line was look within your collar. Did the red pen stay down? Day seven hundred sixty-four.

Lunch at your desk: a sandwich from home, a bit squashed, perfectly fine. Then someone across the room opens a box from the good place down the street, and the smell of it reaches you. The sandwich hasn't changed. It's exactly as good as it was a minute ago. Does it still taste the same? Farid has a pair of couplets about precisely this moment, and they're about bread. Today: dry bread and cool water.
screen: `A SQUASHED SANDWICH, PERFECTLY FINE.` → `A BOX FROM THE GOOD PLACE.` → `THE SANDWICH HASN'T CHANGED.`

segments.voice: Both couplets sit together on Ang 1379. The first, in paraphrase: Farid, my bread is made of wood, and hunger is my relish. Those who eat buttered bread will suffer much pain. Tradition says Farid carried a piece of wood shaped like bread and held it when hunger came, as a discipline. Whatever the story, the line is clear about where the taste comes from: hunger is the seasoning. Then the second couplet, the one in today's index. In paraphrase: eat your dry, plain bread and drink cool water. Farid, don't look at someone else's buttered bread and let your heart long for it. Look closely at what Farid isn't saying. He isn't saying butter is wicked, or that the hungry should be glad to be hungry. Sikh teaching, after all, builds a free kitchen, langar, where everyone is fed. Going hungry is not the goal. The couplet's target is narrower. It's the looking. Dekh, see, and tarsaae, to long, to ache for. The trouble starts when the eyes go across the room to another person's plate, and suddenly your own bread tastes of less. The Punjabi pair for the plain food is rukhi sukhi: dry and simple. Ordinary meals in ordinary homes. And next to it, cool water. Not a luxury, but on a hot day, a real gift. Farid is saying that what's in front of you is enough, if you stop measuring it against someone else's. Envy doesn't add anything to the other plate. It only takes something away from yours.
screen: `MY BREAD IS WOOD; HUNGER IS MY RELISH.` · `NOT AGAINST BUTTER: AGAINST LONGING.` · `THE EYES GO TO ANOTHER'S PLATE.` · `RUKHI SUKHI, AND COOL WATER.` · then, large: `DRY BREAD IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat simply without envy. If you have something plain nearby, a piece of bread, a cracker, a glass of water, use the sit with it. Take one slow bite or one slow sip. Taste it all the way through. When the mind wanders to something better you could be eating, or something someone else has, notice it, and come back to this taste. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Rukhi sukhi. Farid's Punjabi words for dry and plain bread: eat what's in front of you, and don't long for someone else's buttered bread.
Your line: dry bread is enough. Today, at one meal, keep your eyes on your own plate, and taste what's actually there. Day seven hundred sixty-four.

screen: `DAY 764 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE TREE ON THE RIVERBANK.`

765.title: The tree on the riverbank
765.hook: life is a tree on the riverbank; how long can it stand (Farid salok)
765.howItsDone: Farid's saloks are read and sung in gurdwaras with the rest of Gurbani; Sikhs hear in them the Gurus' own reminder that human life is short and precious, a chance to remember the Name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rukhi sukhi: eat what's in front of you, and don't long for another's buttered bread. Your line was dry bread is enough. How did your plain meal taste? Day seven hundred sixty-five.

Rivers in the Punjab move. In the rains they swell, and the water works at the banks all season, quietly carrying the soil away a little at a time. A tree growing right on the edge can look strong for years: thick trunk, wide shade, birds in it. But its roots are in earth the river is slowly taking. Farid looked at a tree like that and saw something about every life. Today: the tree on the riverbank.
screen: `THE RIVER WORKS AT THE BANK.` → `A STRONG TREE ON THE EDGE.` → `FARID SEES A LIFE.`

segments.voice: The couplet, on Ang 1382, in paraphrase: a little tree on the riverbank, how long can it hold firm? Farid, in an unbaked clay pot, how long can water be kept? Two pictures, the same question, and he doesn't answer it. He doesn't need to. Look at the first picture. Farid's word is rukhra, which some readers hear as the little tree, a tender word. He's not sneering at it, and the couplet says nothing against the tree. The trouble isn't in the tree. It's in where every tree stands, on ground that's being carried off. Then the second picture, from a potter's yard. A pot that hasn't been fired in the kiln looks like a pot. You can pour water into it. But the water starts softening the clay from the inside, and before long it seeps out, or the pot gives way. Farid sets the body there: a pot of soft clay, holding something for a while. Some hear this as gloomy. Read it next to his other saloks and it sounds more like a friend's warning. Farid keeps asking a practical question: since the bank won't hold forever, what will you do with the time? Earlier in these days he called himself to rise and pray before dawn; now we can hear why he didn't put it off. Sikhs hear the same note in the Gurus' teaching that a human life is a precious chance, not to be slept through. The tree on the edge isn't a reason for fear. It's a reason to stand well, today, while it stands.
screen: `HOW LONG CAN THE TREE HOLD FIRM?` · `RUKHRA — THE LITTLE TREE.` · `WATER IN AN UNBAKED POT.` · `NOT GLOOM: WHAT WILL YOU DO WITH THE TIME?` · then, large: `HOW LONG CAN IT STAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand by water. If you can, stand near water now, a sink, a glass, a window with rain, a fountain, a river if you're lucky. If not, picture the riverbank. Stand, feet planted, like the tree. Feel your weight on the ground. Breathe. Let the question come, without any fear in it: while I'm standing, what's worth doing today? Wait for one plain answer. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Rukhra. Farid's little tree on the riverbank: strong, giving shade, and standing on ground the river is slowly taking.
Your line: how long can it stand. Today, do the one thing your answer named, before the day carries it away. Day seven hundred sixty-five.

766.title: Every heart a jewel
766.hook: don't speak one harsh word; the Master is in all; don't break any heart, every heart is a jewel (Farid salok, ang 1384)
766.howItsDone: Farid's saloks are read and sung in gurdwaras with the rest of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs read this couplet together with the Gurus' teaching that the one light of God is in all people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rukhra: strong, giving shade, on ground the river is taking. Your line was how long can it stand. Did you do the one thing your answer named? Day seven hundred sixty-six.

A jeweler's counter. The stones sit on black velvet, and nobody handles them roughly. Even the person who sweeps the shop at night knows to be careful near that glass. A thing that precious changes how everyone moves around it, and how they speak near it, too. Farid takes that picture and sets it down somewhere unexpected: inside every person you'll talk to today, including the ones who annoy you. Today: every heart a jewel.
screen: `STONES ON BLACK VELVET.` → `NOBODY HANDLES THEM ROUGHLY.` → `INSIDE EVERY PERSON.`

segments.voice: The couplets are on Ang 1384, near the end of Farid's saloks. The first, in paraphrase: don't speak even one harsh word; the True Master lives in everyone. Don't break anyone's heart; all of them are priceless jewels. We heard that line once in year one. Today, look at two things in it. First, the word for harsh. Farid's word is phika. It means flat, tasteless, without sweetness, like food with no salt. So the harsh word isn't only a shout. It's also the cold, flat word: the curt reply, the sigh, the answer with nothing kind in it. Two days ago, Farid's bread was plain and enough. A plain word is fine. A word with the sweetness drained out on purpose is what Farid warns against. Second, the reason. He doesn't say be nice because it's polite. He says the True Master is in everyone. Speak flatly to a person and you're speaking that way to the place where the Lord lives. Then the next couplet pushes it further, in paraphrase: every mind is a jewel, and breaking one is not good at all. If you long for your Beloved, don't break anyone's heart. That's the turn. For Farid, love of God and care for people aren't two projects. The longing for the Beloved is exactly what forbids the harsh word. You can't want the jeweler and smash the jewels. Sikhs hear this beside the Gurus' own teaching that one light is in all, and they sing Farid's couplet in that light. A Sufi's line, kept in the Sikh scripture, on how to speak to anyone at all.
screen: `DON'T SPEAK ONE HARSH WORD.` · `PHIKA — FLAT, WITHOUT SWEETNESS.` · `THE TRUE MASTER IS IN EVERYONE.` · `LONG FOR THE BELOVED; BREAK NO HEART.` · then, large: `EVERY HEART A JEWEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak no harsh word today. In the sit, think through who you'll speak with before tonight. Family, a coworker, a stranger at a counter, someone online. Pause on the one you're most likely to be flat with. Picture the jewel on black velvet, there, inside them. Then try one ordinary sentence you'll say to them, silently, twice: once flat, once with a little sweetness left in it. Hear the difference. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Phika. Farid's word for the harsh, flat word without sweetness: don't speak it, because the True Master lives in everyone and every heart is a priceless jewel.
Your line: add one grain of sweetness. Today, when a flat word is ready on your tongue, let a little kindness go with it before it leaves. Day seven hundred sixty-six.

767.title: Farid close
767.hook: a Sufi's humility near the end of the Guru's book: become the grass on the path
767.howItsDone: Farid's couplets are read and sung in gurdwaras as gurbani alongside the Gurus' own hymns, and Sikhs often draw on them when speaking about nimrata, humility.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Farid asked us not to break a single heart, because every heart is a jewel. Your line was add one grain of sweetness. Did a harsh word stay unspoken? Day seven hundred sixty-seven.

Turn toward the last pages of the Guru Granth Sahib, among the short couplets, and a Muslim saint of the Punjab is still speaking there, signing his lines with his own name: Farid. For a week this path has sat with him. A tree on a riverbank. A heart like a jewel. Dry bread and cool water. A collar to look under before judging anyone else. Today we close his pages. And the last thing to hear from him sits under all the others: how low a person is willing to go.
screen: `A SUFI NEAR THE END OF THE BOOK.` → `A WEEK WITH FARID.` → `HOW LOW WILL YOU GO?`

segments.voice: Here is one of Farid's couplets, in paraphrase, from Ang 1378. Farid, if you long for the Lord of all, become the grass on the path. One person cuts it, another tramples it. Then you'll be let into the Master's court. Grass by a footpath doesn't argue. It doesn't keep a list of who walked on it. It gets cut and grows back. It's low enough that nobody notices it, and steady enough that the path stays green. Farid asks to be that. Now, a careful second turn. Some readers worry this sounds like letting people walk all over you. But look at the Farid of this whole week. The same man told us to look under our own collar, and said that those with one thing in the heart and another on the lips are false. That isn't a doormat talking. His humility is sharp. It's the self that insists on being seen that he wants to lower, not the truth he's willing to say. The third turn is about where these lines live. A Sufi of the Punjab, and his couplets sit inside the book Sikhs bow to as their living Guru. Sikhs have a word for the quality Farid keeps returning to: nimrata, humility. Tradition says the Gurus treasured his verses, and the book keeps them near its close, in his own Punjabi, with his name in the lines. So the week ends where Farid's pages keep pointing. Not with a crown. With grass, and a path, and a door that opens for the one who's willing to be low. Humble to the end.
screen: `BECOME THE GRASS ON THE PATH.` · `CUT, TRAMPLED, GROWING BACK.` · `HUMBLE, BUT NOT SILENT.` · `HIS NAME IN THE LINES.` · then, large: `HUMBLE TO THE END.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read Farid once more. Choose one of his lines from this week. The tree on the riverbank. Every heart a jewel. Dry bread and cool water. Look under your own collar. Or the grass on the path. Say it slowly, once, and then sit with it. Let your breath go out longer than it comes in, the way grass bends. If one line keeps tugging at you, that's the one to keep. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Nimrata. Humility, the quality Farid's couplets keep returning to: not a crown, but grass that lets itself be cut and trampled, steady enough to keep the path green.
Your line: humble to the end. Today, let one small thing go without needing credit for it, and say nothing about it. Day seven hundred sixty-seven.

768.title: The calico printer
768.hook: Namdev, a cloth-printer and devotee of Maharashtra, sings with his trade's own tools: the measuring yard, the scissors, the dye
768.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Namdev's hymns as gurbani, and his picture of praying through ordinary work is often linked to the Sikh ideals of kirat karni, honest work, and naam japna, remembering the Name.

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed Farid's pages with nimrata, the grass on the path. Your line was humble to the end. Did one small thing go by without your needing credit? Day seven hundred sixty-eight.

A wooden block, carved with a pattern. A tray of dye. A length of plain cotton laid flat on a table. Press, lift, move along, press again, until the cloth is covered in flowers. That's calico printing by hand, and tradition says it was the family trade of Namdev, a devotee from Maharashtra, far to the south of the Punjab. His hymns sit in the Guru Granth Sahib. And in one of them he doesn't leave his workshop to pray. He prays with the tools still in his hands.
screen: `A BLOCK, A DYE, A LENGTH OF CLOTH.` → `NAMDEV OF MAHARASHTRA.` → `PRAYING WITH THE TOOLS IN HAND.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Asa, on Ang 485. Here it is in paraphrase. My mind is the measuring yard, and my tongue is the scissors. I measure and measure, and cut away the noose of death. What do I care about caste, what do I care about lineage? I repeat the Lord's Name day and night. I dye what is to be dyed, I sew what is to be sewn, and without the Name I can't live for even a moment. Hear what he's doing. Every tool on the table becomes a way of remembering. The measuring yard is the mind, taking the measure of things. The tongue that says the Name is the scissors, cutting what binds him. The dye vat and the needle stay in use, and the Name runs through all of it. Here's the second turn. Right in the middle of that workshop, Namdev asks what caste and lineage have to do with any of this. Some people of his time counted a printer of cloth as low. Namdev doesn't argue the ranking. He just walks past it, because the Name doesn't ask what family you came from. And the third turn is about the Sikh book that keeps this hymn. The Gurus taught kirat karni, earning by honest work, and naam japna, remembering the Name. Namdev's workshop holds both in one room. He isn't a monk who left the table. He's a craftsman who made the table holy. So a prayer doesn't need new words here. It can be the old motions of your day, done with the One in mind. A printer's prayer.
screen: `MY MIND THE YARD, MY TONGUE THE SCISSORS.` · `WHAT DO I CARE ABOUT CASTE?` · `DYEING AND SEWING, WITH THE NAME.` · `WORK AND REMEMBRANCE, ONE ROOM.` · then, large: `A PRINTER'S PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: print or stamp something by hand. A thumb pressed in ink or coffee on a scrap of paper. A potato cut into a shape. A rubber stamp, a fingertip, a leaf. Press, lift, press again, slowly, and let each press be one breath. Don't aim for pretty. Notice your hands, the pressure, the mark left behind. If you're somewhere you can't make a mark, press your thumb gently into your palm instead. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with each press. The bell holds the time.
Chhipa. The calico printer's trade tradition gives to Namdev, who prays with the tools still in his hands: the yard, the scissors, the dye.
Your line: a printer's prayer. Today, pick one tool you use every day, a pen, a spoon, a keyboard, and let it remind you once of the Name. Day seven hundred sixty-eight.

769.title: The milk offering
769.hook: Namdev sings of offering a cup of milk and pleading until the Lord drank it (Bhairao, Namdev, ang 1163)
769.howItsDone: Namdev's milk hymn is sung in kirtan as gurbani, and Sikhs often tell it as a story about loving trust, while Sikh practice itself makes no food offerings to images.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chhipa: Namdev with his mind as the measuring yard and his tongue as the scissors. Your line was a printer's prayer. Which tool reminded you? Day seven hundred sixty-nine.

Drink this milk. That's the heart of the prayer, said by someone standing before the Lord with a cup of fresh milk and a jug of water, waiting for it to be drunk. And he pleads. Tradition remembers him as a boy. But the pleading isn't a story told about Namdev by someone else. It's a hymn in his own voice, in Raag Bhairao, in the Guru Granth Sahib. Today: the milk offering.
screen: `DRINK THIS MILK.` → `HE WAITS, AND PLEADS.` → `IN NAMDEV'S OWN VOICE.`

segments.voice: The hymn is on Ang 1163. Here it is in paraphrase. Namdev milked the brown cow and brought a cup of milk and a jug of water. Drink this milk, Gobind Rai, he says, and my mind will be at peace. If you don't, my father at home will be angry with me. And then, the hymn says, the Lord looked on Namdev, smiled, and drank the milk, and Namdev went home having seen the Lord. Tradition fills in the setting: his father, away for the day, left the boy in charge of the offering. The hymn itself needs no more than that cup. Look at what the boy doesn't do. He doesn't know a ceremony. He doesn't argue about whether God drinks milk. He brings the best thing he has, fresh from the cow, and he simply expects it to be received. His worry is a child's worry: I'll be in trouble at home. And it's that plain, stubborn trust that the hymn says was answered. Here's the second turn. Sikhs read a hymn like this in more than one way. Some hear a real wonder. Others hear a picture of what love does to distance: when the heart offers without holding back, the Lord is not far off. The hymn doesn't stop to explain. It just says, he drank the milk. And the third turn is about offerings now. The Gurus taught that the Lord wants love more than ritual. Namdev's cup is a small offering, milk from the brown cow, and it's the one the hymn remembers. He drank the milk.
screen: `THE BROWN COW, THE CUP, THE JUG.` · `DRINK THIS, GOBIND RAI.` · `NO CEREMONY, ONLY TRUST.` · `A WONDER, OR LOVE CLOSING THE DISTANCE.` · then, large: `HE DRANK THE MILK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer something simply. Pour a glass of water, or hold whatever is in reach, a cup of tea, an apple, a flower. Set it down in front of you. Sit, and breathe. Don't add words or a ceremony. Just offer it, the way the boy set down his cup, and wait in the quiet without needing anything to happen. When the bell sounds, drink the water, or share the thing with someone. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you set it down. The bell holds the time.
Gobind Rai. Namdev's name for the Lord in his hymn: drink this milk, he pleaded, and the Lord smiled and drank it.
Your line: he drank the milk. Today, give one thing, a cup, a meal, an hour, simply, without explaining it. Day seven hundred sixty-nine.

770.title: The temple turned
770.hook: turned away from a temple for his low caste, Namdev sang, and the hymn says the temple turned to face him (Malar, Namdev)
770.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Namdev's Malar hymn as gurbani and often tell the turning of the temple when speaking about the Gurus' rejection of caste, which gurdwaras express in langar, where everyone sits and eats together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gobind Rai: a boy, a cup, and a Lord who drank. Your line was he drank the milk. What did you give, simply? Day seven hundred seventy.

Laughing, playing, a man walks up to a temple to sing. Before he gets far, someone grabs him and hauls him out. The reason is his family. He's a printer of cloth, and the ones who throw him out count that as low. He picks up his blanket, walks around to the back of the building, and sits down by the rear wall. It could end there. This story, told by Namdev in his own hymn, is only getting started.
screen: `LAUGHING, HE COMES TO SING.` → `HAULED OUT FOR HIS CASTE.` → `HE SITS BEHIND THE TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Malar, on Ang 1292. In paraphrase, Namdev says: laughing and playing, I came to your temple. While I was worshipping, I was seized and thrown out. Low is my caste, O Lord. Why was I born a printer of cloth? I picked up my blanket and went back, and sat behind the temple. And then the turn. As Namdev sang the Lord's praises, the temple turned around to face the devotee. Hear the question in the middle of it. Why was I born a printer? It's honest. It's the hurt of a man shut out for something he never chose. The hymn doesn't pretend it didn't sting. Then look at what he does with it. He doesn't break the door down. He doesn't stop singing. He sits at the back wall and keeps praising. And in the hymn, the building moves to him. Notice who the hymn follows. The ones who threw him out get one line and then drop out of it. Everything after that is a man singing and a Lord who listens. The building that had its back to him ends up facing him, and the one who was thrown out is now the one at the front. This turn ends our week, and it's the plainest picture of it: low, honest, and received. The temple turned.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome someone left outside. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind a person at the edge of your circle. The quiet coworker nobody invites. The relative who doesn't get the call. The neighbor who eats alone. Hold their face for a few breaths, the way the temple turned to face Namdev. Then choose one small way to turn toward them this week: a message, a seat saved, a question asked and listened to. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with their name. The bell holds the time.
Dehura. The temple in Namdev's hymn, which turned to face him after he was thrown out and sat singing at the back wall.
Your line: low, honest, and received. Today, be the one who turns toward the person at the back of the room. Day seven hundred seventy.
